entries.note: False outputs are publicly testable, but the categorical absence of an intent to deceive cannot be established from outputs alone.

entries.test: Public controlled studies of GPT's errors and factual representations could test whether its false outputs arise from inadequate factual knowledge.
entries.note: Read in context, 'doesn't know any better' offers a functional explanation of factual errors.

entries.test: Public model documentation and controlled experiments varying training-data size and coverage could test the claimed explanation of true and false completions.
entries.note: The causal explanation is testable even if it is oversimplified or incorrect.

entries.test: Public factual-accuracy evaluations and reproducible examples of GPT generating false statements would test whether it is reliable as a source of factual truth.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion gives 'trusted' a plain factual-reliability meaning.

entries.test: Public mechanistic studies of GPT falsehoods and human deception could establish whether the proposed categorical separation holds.
entries.note: Marcus says similar outputs do not establish similar mechanisms; the proposition strengthens this into a categorical claim of unrelated mechanisms and generalizes from Santos to humans.
